title: Of False Evidence and Offences Against Public Justice
shortDescription: Offences that corrupt the justice system: perjury and fabricated evidence, false certificates and declarations, destroying evidence and screening offenders, fraud on courts, false criminal charges, harbouring offenders, public servants who pervert justice or let prisoners escape, resisting arrest and escape, breaking remission conditions, insulting courts and jumping bail.

subHeadings.label: Fraud on courts and false charges
Public servants perverting justice or allowing escape
Resisting arrest, escape, remission, court insult and bail

summary:
Chapter XIV is the largest chapter on the administration of justice. It protects the truth-finding process of courts and the machinery of arrest, custody and punishment. It corresponds to Chapter XI of the IPC (ss.191-229A), and the BNS sections follow the IPC order closely: s.227 = s.191, s.228 = s.192, and so on up to s.269 = s.229A. The Gazette gives the chapter no sub-headings; its 43 sections fall into six groups: false evidence (ss.227-237), destroying evidence and withholding information (ss.238-241), fraud on courts and false charges (ss.242-248), harbouring and screening offenders (ss.249-254), public servants perverting justice or allowing escape (ss.255-261), and resisting arrest, escape and related offences (ss.262-269).

Sections 227 and 228 are definitions. Giving false evidence (perjury) is making a false statement, known or believed to be false, while legally bound to tell the truth by oath, law or a duty to make a declaration; a false statement about one's own belief counts. Fabricating false evidence is creating a false circumstance, entry, document or electronic record intending it to mislead a court, public servant or arbitrator on a material point. Section 229 punishes both — up to seven years and fine up to ₹10,000 in a judicial proceeding (widely defined to include court-martials and court-directed investigations), and up to three years and fine up to ₹5,000 otherwise. False evidence aimed at a capital conviction carries life or ten years (s.230), and death if an innocent person is executed; aimed at a conviction for an offence punishable with life or seven years or more, the offender faces that offence's punishment (s.231). Threatening a witness into giving false evidence carries up to seven years (s.232). Sections 233-237 apply the false-evidence punishment to knowingly using false evidence, issuing or using false certificates, and making or using false declarations receivable as evidence.

Sections 238-241 deal with cover-ups: causing evidence to disappear or giving false information to screen an offender (graded by the gravity of the original offence), failing to give legally required information about an offence, giving false information about an offence, and destroying documents or electronic records to prevent their production. Sections 242-247 target fraud on the courts: false personation in a suit or prosecution, hiding or transferring property to defeat forfeiture, fines or decrees, fraudulent claims to such property, collusive or false decrees, and knowingly false claims in court. Section 248 punishes instituting criminal proceedings or making a false charge with intent to injure, knowing there is no just ground — now up to five years (or a ₹2 lakh fine), and up to ten years for false charges of grave offences.

Sections 249-254 punish those who help offenders escape justice: harbouring an offender, taking or giving gratification to conceal an offence (not applicable to compoundable offences), taking a fee to recover stolen property without helping catch the thief, harbouring escapees or persons ordered to be arrested, and harbouring robbers or dacoits. Spouses are exempt from the harbouring offences. Sections 255-261 address public servants: disobeying the law or framing incorrect records to save an offender, corruptly making judicial orders contrary to law, unlawful commitment or confinement, and intentionally or negligently allowing an accused or convict to escape. Sections 262-265 punish resisting one's own or another's lawful arrest, escaping, and rescuing prisoners. The chapter closes with breach of conditional remission (s.266), insulting or interrupting a public servant sitting in a judicial proceeding (s.267), personation of an assessor (s.268), and failure of a person released on bail to appear in court (s.269), which is cognizable and non-bailable. None of the Chapter's offences is listed as compoundable.
